<reason>Both sides argued competently and answered pressure questions in proper format, but A built the more durable path to victory. A's key structural move—distinguishing "suffering remains open to intervention until death" from "death forecloses correction permanently"—survived Rebuttal 1 unanswered after B's "irreversibility cuts both ways" line, and B never returned to contest that specific distinction in Rebuttal 2 or Closing. More decisively, when B answered the Q2 pressure question with three safeguard features (constitutional entrenchment, sunset clauses, diagnosis-anchoring), A turned the strongest of these against B in Rebuttal 2: it was precisely constitutional/Charter equality-autonomy reasoning that Canadian courts used to strike the "reasonably foreseeable death" line, meaning entrenchment is the mechanism of drift, not a defense against it. B's Closing reasserted the suffering-vs-diagnosis distinction but did not engage this boomerang point at all, leaving a live, decisive rebuttal unanswered. B's closing pivot to framing A's honest concession ("I don't claim this reaches zero residual suffering") as "the whole motion" was rhetorically sharp but somewhat overclaimed, since A had explicitly reframed the comparison to systemic/category-level effects rather than the single-patient frame B needed to sustain that reading. The debate was close and both sides argued the actual motion cleanly, but A's rebuttal architecture held up better under the final exchange.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 2 turn of B's own proposed safeguard—constitutional entrenchment—into evidence that courts, using the same autonomy/equality logic PRO's case depends on, are exactly what expanded Canada's law; B's Closing never directly answered this point.</best_rebuttal>
